notes: Parole Board recall JR; procedural unfairness from non-disclosure and inadequate reasons is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Parole Board recall quashed for procedural unfairness
key_facts: The claimant was sentenced for serious sexual offences against his step-daughter, released on licence after serving two-thirds of his sentence, and recalled after failing to cooperate with a Sex Offender Treatment Programme.
He challenged the Parole Board's October 2003 rejection of his representations against recall.
Material describing his SOTP non-cooperation was not disclosed to him or his representatives before the Board's decision.
The Board's reasons were brief and did not address his argument that requiring treatment while he denied guilt was unreasonable.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim to quash the Parole Board's decision rejecting representations against recall to prison.
enrichment.outcome: Decision quashed; matter to be reconsidered at an imminent Parole Board review with full material; claimant awarded three-quarters of costs.
enrichment.ratio: A recalled prisoner is entitled to a fair hearing on representations against recall; failure to disclose relevant material and inadequacy of reasons addressing a central issue (whether SOTP attendance was a reasonable licence requirement given denial of guilt) renders the Parole Board's decision procedurally defective even where recall may ultimately be justified.
legal_issues: Whether non-disclosure of the SOTP report rendered the recall decision unfair
Whether the Parole Board's reasons were adequate
Whether a licence condition requiring sex offender treatment could lawfully be enforced where the licensee denied guilt
Whether automatic release at two-thirds affected the reasonableness of such conditions
linked_authorities: The Queen on the application of Wilkes v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2001] EWHC Admin 210

confidence.notes: Procedural grounds for quashing and reconsideration order are explicit. Substantive reasonableness of the licence condition was not finally decided.

notes: Litigant-in-person JR of civil case management orders; abuse of process reasoning is straightforward.

enrichment.short_title: Judicial review of civil orders refused as abuse of process
key_facts: Mr Kumar, a litigant in person, sought judicial review of case management and strike-out orders in two civil claims against the Home Office and Staffordshire University Students Union.
His personal injury claim against the Home Office was ultimately struck out by Poole J after earlier interlocutory orders he now attacked.
His libel claim against the Students Union was struck out for having no foundation.
He had a right of appeal against each terminating order but did not pursue appeals.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to proceed with a judicial review claim attacking County Court and High Court case management decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; the claim was manifestly an abuse of process because adequate appellate remedies existed.
enrichment.ratio: Decisions made in civil proceedings in the County Court or High Court are not ordinarily amenable to judicial review where the claimant had and failed to use a right of appeal; using the Administrative Court to attack such orders is an abuse of process.
legal_issues: Whether interlocutory and strike-out orders in civil proceedings are reviewable in the Administrative Court
Whether pending or unused rights of appeal preclude judicial review
Whether exceptional circumstances existed to justify prerogative review of civil court decisions

confidence.notes: Abuse of process conclusion and factual chronology are clearly stated. No complex statutory construction involved.

notes: Detailed contempt findings on freezing and search order breaches; liability analysis is complete though sentencing is not in the text.

enrichment.short_title: Contempt for breach of freezing and search orders in mobile phone fraud case
key_facts: Nokia sued to recover mobile telephones sold through a chain involving Cybertech and Ibericatel, alleging a retention-of-title fraud.
Morison J granted worldwide freezing and search orders against Interstone Trading Ltd and director Mr Jin Yan in November 2003.

Mr Yan failed to disclose extensive Hong Kong assets when questioned, shredded a document relating to Zhongfang Tianxing, and attempted to conceal other relevant papers during the Interstone office search.
His formal asset declarations were seriously incomplete despite legal advice.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to commit Mr Yan to prison for contempt for breaches of freezing and search orders.
enrichment.outcome: Contempt established in multiple respects; deliberate non-disclosure of foreign assets and document destruction were particularly serious; post-transfer payments were held to fall within the ordinary course of business exception.
enrichment.ratio: A respondent served with a standard-form worldwide freezing order must disclose assets to the best of his ability immediately; deliberate suppression of foreign assets, shredding of relevant documents, and concealment during a search constitute contempt, proved to the criminal standard; the applicant bears the burden of proving breaches of the freezing order beyond ordinary business exceptions.
legal_issues: Whether Mr Yan deliberately failed to disclose foreign assets on 13 November 2003
Whether document shredding and concealment during the search amounted to contempt
Whether formal disclosure affidavits were materially defective
Whether post-order bank transfers breached the freezing injunction
Whether scheduled search-order documents remained undisclosed

confidence.notes: Detailed findings on liability are in the judgment. The published text ends after liability conclusions and does not record any committal sentence.

notes: Limitation Act s.32(1)(b) deliberate concealment analysis is thorough; split on Mr Brown's state of mind does not affect outcome.

enrichment.short_title: Solicitor negligence limitation: deliberate concealment of consent order
key_facts: Ms Williams instructed FP&H after a stroke allegedly caused by inappropriate prescription of Femodene.
Solicitor Mr Brown consented without instructions to an order dismissing Dr Salahuddin from the claim on 25 August 1994, destroying her chance to sue the doctor.
Mr Brown did not tell Ms Williams about the consent order for many months while unsuccessfully trying to revive the claim.
She issued a negligence claim against FP&H in December 2000, outside the ordinary six-year period from August 1994.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a preliminary issue trial holding the claim time-barred under the Limitation Act 1980.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; claim not statute-barred because s.32(1)(b) postponed limitation until Ms Williams discovered the concealed consent order.
enrichment.ratio: Under s.32(1)(b), deliberate concealment by a solicitor of facts relevant to the client's right of action—including consent to dismissal of the underlying claim—postpones limitation until discovery; concealment motivated by embarrassment rather than intent to hide a negligence claim still satisfies the provision, and the defendant need not have appreciated that the fact was legally relevant to a claim against the firm.
legal_issues: Whether s.32(1)(b) applied to Mr Brown's non-disclosure of the consent order
Whether deliberate concealment requires intent to prevent a negligence claim
When the limitation period began to run
Relationship between s.32(1)(b) and the House of Lords decision in Cave v Robinson Jarvis & Rolf
index_terms: Cave v Robinson Jarvis and Rolf
linked_authorities: Sheldon v RHM Outhwaite (Underwriting Agencies) Ltd [1996] AC 102
Cave v Robinson Jarvis & Rolf [2003] 1 AC 384
Brocklesby v Armitage & Guest [2002] 1 WLR 598
Beaman v ARTS Ltd [1949] 1 KB 550

confidence.notes: Majority reasoning on s.32(1)(b) and appeal outcome are explicit. Minor disagreement on fact-finding about Mr Brown's awareness does not affect the result.

notes: Registered IPS dissolution and member entitlement analysis is detailed and coherent.

enrichment.short_title: Distribution of assets of defunct Luton Labour Club
key_facts: The Luton Labour Club and Institute Ltd, a registered industrial and provident society, suspended activities in 1997 and sold its George Street premises for about £300,000.
The management committee resigned and subscriptions were not collected after 1997, though some members' cheques were returned.
The Registrar cancelled registration on 31 March 2000 on the basis the society had ceased to exist.
A fund of about £271,000 remained for distribution among competing life members, ordinary members, and unverified claimants.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery application to determine how the club's remaining assets should be distributed and who qualifies as a member.
enrichment.outcome: Distribution date fixed at 31 March 2000; paid-up ordinary members at end December 1997 may participate; further membership claims to be evaluated; trustees appointed subject to fitness affidavits.
enrichment.ratio: A registered industrial and provident society remains a corporate body owning its assets beneficially until formal dissolution or cancellation of registration; spontaneous dissolution principles for unincorporated clubs do not apply before cancellation; where a club suspended activities and did not collect subscriptions, ordinary members who were paid up when activities ceased remain entitled despite expulsive non-payment rules.
legal_issues: When the registered society ceased to exist for distribution purposes
Whether ordinary members lost membership for non-payment of 1998 subscriptions
Whether unincorporated association spontaneous dissolution principles applied
What investigations were required for unverified membership claims

enrichment.short_title: Land sale overage: parking spaces included in residential unit prices

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Use Classes) Order 1987

key_facts: Bride Hall Estates sold Aldersgate Street property to St George on terms requiring residential development and overage at 35% of sale proceeds above £340 per sq ft of net internal area.
The development comprised 81 apartments and 41 parking spaces, mostly sold with flats for a single price.
St George sought to deduct about £823,000 attributed to parking from aggregate residential sale prices, reducing overage payable.
A preliminary issue asked whether parking sums formed part of aggregate sale prices under clause 11.4.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a Deputy High Court Judge's reversal of a Deputy Master's decision on a preliminary contractual construction issue.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; parking space payments are included in aggregate sale prices for overage calculation and may not be deducted.
enrichment.ratio: On the true construction of the development agreement, 'Residential Units' and aggregate sale prices include associated car parking appurtenant to apartments; exclusion of parking from net internal area is a measurement rule for the threshold formula, not a valuation rule excluding parking from gross sale prices.
legal_issues: Whether aggregate sale prices for Residential Units include sums paid for parking spaces
Effect of the Net Internal Area definition excluding car parking
Whether parking could theoretically be sold separately affects overage calculation
Relevance of subsequent sale events to contractual construction

confidence.notes: Preliminary issue answer and contractual pointers are clearly explained. Judge's reliance on subsequent sale events was rejected but did not change the outcome.

enrichment.short_title: VAT on seasonal static caravan pitches upheld
key_facts: Colaingrove Ltd let concrete seasonal pitches with utilities for static caravans used mainly for holidays.
Licences typically ran eight years but prohibited permanent residence and overnight stays December to February.
HMRC treated the supplies as standard-rated under the exclusion for seasonal caravan pitches in Schedule 9 Group 1.
The VAT Tribunal and Jacob J upheld VAT; Colaingrove appealed on Sixth Directive compatibility.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from High Court dismissal of appeal against VAT Tribunal decision imposing VAT on pitch licences.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; UK exclusion of seasonal caravan pitches from the lettings exemption is compatible with Article 13B(b); no reference to the ECJ as acte clair.
enrichment.ratio: Member States may use the Article 13B(b) tailpiece option to exclude further lettings from the immovable property exemption where reasonably identifying non-dwelling holiday use; the UK seasonal pitch test, including 'no sleep' restrictions, is a proportionate means of aligning static caravan sites with taxable holiday accommodation.
legal_issues: Scope of the Article 13B(b) member state option to restrict lettings exemptions
Whether seasonal static caravan pitches are taxable holiday rather than exempt residential lettings
Whether the UK regime discriminates against caravan licensees compared with hotel long-stays
Whether a reference to the ECJ was required

enrichment.short_title: Permission to appeal residence order relocation refused
key_facts: A father applied for a residence order to move 11-year-old E from Kent to live with him in Northern Ireland, separating him from his 16-year-old brother T.
A CAFCASS officer recommended the move, finding special circumstances and serious risks in refusing E's strongly held wish.
HHJ Andrews granted the residence order on 30 January 2004 with implementation during half-term.
The mother sought permission to appeal and a stay seven days before the move.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal and stay of a residence order made at Canterbury County Court.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal and stay refused; no order for costs.
enrichment.ratio: An appellate court should not grant permission or stay where the trial judge properly relied on CAFCASS evidence, adequately considered sibling separation and contact enforcement, and gave appropriate weight to a mature child's wishes; late fresh evidence did not undermine the judge's reasoning.
legal_issues: Whether the judge adequately considered impact of separating the brothers
Whether contact orders after relocation would be illusory given the father's record
Whether too much weight was given to an 11-year-old's wishes
Whether half-term implementation timing was wrong

confidence.notes: Outcome and core reasoning are clear in a brief extempore-style judgment. Detailed welfare evaluation rests on the first-instance judge and CAFCASS report not fully reproduced.

notes: Complex Enterprise Act merger reference test and CAT judicial review; appeal dismissed on mixed grounds with dense competition analysis.

enrichment.short_title: iSoft-Torex merger: OFT no-reference decision restored on review
key_facts: iSoft offered to acquire Torex, creating a relevant merger situation in NHS healthcare IT software with substantial combined legacy market shares.
OFT decided in November 2003 not to refer the merger to the Competition Commission, relying heavily on the transformative effect of the NHS National Programme for IT.
IBA Healthcare challenged the decision; the Competition Appeal Tribunal quashed it for applying the wrong s.33 test and inadequate reasoning.
OFT, iSoft and Torex appealed; the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, upholding CAT's quashing order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on points of law from Competition Appeal Tribunal review of OFT decision not to refer an anticipated merger under Enterprise Act 2002 section 33.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; CAT's decision to quash OFT's no-reference decision and remit for reconsideration upheld; correct test is whether OFT reasonably believed the merger may result in a substantial lessening of competition, not a two-stage 'room for two views' test.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 33(1) Enterprise Act 2002 OFT must form its own reasonable belief whether a merger may be expected to result in a substantial lessening of competition; CAT erred in requiring OFT additionally to exclude any credible Commission alternative view, but OFT's decision was nevertheless vitiated because it failed adequately to justify rejecting serious legacy-market competition concerns in light of NPfIT uncertainty.
legal_issues: Correct interpretation of 'believes that it is or may be the case' in section 33(1)
Whether CAT's two-part 'room for two views' test was lawful
Application of judicial review principles under section 120(4)
Whether OFT adequately reasoned its conclusion that NPfIT negated a substantial lessening of competition

Edwards v Bairstow [1956] AC 14

enrichment.short_title: Housing benefit overpayment must deduct underlying entitlement
key_facts: Mrs Adan received housing benefit while on income support but failed to report starting hotel work in January 1998.
Hounslow identified overpayments for June-December 1998; if her change had been reported she would have been entitled to about £2,400 of the £3,000 paid.
The authority sought to recover the full overpayment without deducting underlying benefit.
The appeal tribunal and Commissioner followed R v Wyre BC ex parte Lord that 'properly payable' required a valid backdated claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Social Security Commissioner dismissal of appeal against local authority overpayment recovery decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; ex parte Lord wrongly decided; recoverable overpayment must be calculated after deducting benefit properly payable on true facts via Regulation 79 review, without requiring a fresh claim.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation 104(a) requires deduction of amounts properly payable on the claimant's true circumstances when calculating recoverable overpayment; 'properly payable' is not synonymous with strict 'entitlement' and does not require a separately submitted backdated claim, including where loss of income support ended the benefit period.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'properly payable' in Regulation 104(a) pre-October 2000 amendment
Whether underlying entitlement must be established by a valid claim before set-off
Interaction between Regulations 67, 72, 79 and 104 where income support ceases
Whether ex parte Lord should be followed
linked_authorities: R v Wyre Borough Council ex parte Lord (24 October 1997)
Secretary of State for Work and Pensions v Chiltern District Council [2003] EWCA Civ 508
Morton v Chief Adjudication Officer [1988] IRLR 444

confidence.notes: Appellate overruling of ex parte Lord and remittal for recalculation are explicit. Council tax parallel regulations were not fully argued.
